title: “DRAW NEAR TO GOD, AND HE WILL DRAW NEAR TO YOU” — BUT THE VERY NEXT WORDS ARE THE ONES WE KEEP AVOIDING
paragraphs: “DRAW NEAR TO GOD, AND HE WILL DRAW NEAR TO YOU” — BUT THE VERY NEXT WORDS ARE THE ONES WE KEEP AVOIDING

We love the promise of God's presence. But James 4:8 doesn't end with an invitation to feel closer to heaven. It continues with a command that confronts the sin we've learned to hide. And what comes after that may change the way you understand repentance, brokenness, and the grace of Jesus Christ forever.
There is something deeply unsettling about reading a Bible verse you've loved for years… and suddenly realizing you stopped reading right before it confronted you.
You highlighted the promise.
You memorized it.
You whispered it during sleepless nights when heaven felt silent and your prayers seemed to hit the ceiling.
“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”
Beautiful words.
Comforting words.

Words that have carried exhausted Christians through hospital corridors, broken marriages, financial disasters, unanswered prayers, and seasons when faith felt like the last fragile thread holding their lives together.
But what if I told you that the very next words are not the comforting embrace many people expect?
What if the same verse that invites you closer to God also exposes the very things keeping your heart divided?
And what if that exposure is not God pushing you away…
…but His mercy calling you home?
Because James did not stop where our favorite inspirational graphics usually stop.
He continued.
And what he wrote next should make every one of us examine our hearts.
James 4:8 says:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Slowly.
The same verse that says God will draw near also says, “Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.”
There it is.
The part that doesn't fit neatly on a coffee mug.
The part that interrupts our carefully managed religious image.
The part that confronts the person who wants God's comfort without surrendering the sin that is destroying them.
And before you think this is about somebody else…
Remember how easy it is to recognize another person's compromise while defending our own.
We can condemn dishonesty while hiding the truth.
We can sing about forgiveness while secretly feeding resentment.
We can pray for purity while protecting habits we know are poisoning our minds.
We can ask God to bless our relationships while refusing to apologize to the people we've wounded.
We can raise our hands in worship on Sunday and use those same hands to tear someone apart with our words on Monday.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not that we have stopped believing in God.
It is that we have learned how to speak His language while resisting His authority.
James is writing to people who know the language of faith.
People who understand religious practices.
People who have heard about God.
And yet their communities are being damaged by envy, selfish ambition, quarrels, and desires that have become more important than obedience.
In James 4:1, he asks where their conflicts come from.
His answer is painfully personal.
The battle outside is connected to desires waging war inside.
By James 4:4, he uses the shocking language of spiritual adultery to confront friendship with the world.
He is not saying that loving people outside the church is wrong. Jesus Himself ate with sinners and came to seek and save the lost.
James is confronting allegiance to a system of desires that opposes God.
A heart that wants God's name attached to a life still governed by pride, envy, and selfish ambition.
Then comes the breathtaking promise of James 4:6:
“But he giveth more grace.”
More grace.
Not less grace.
Not a declaration that every struggling believer is beyond hope.
More grace.
But James immediately reminds us that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
Then he calls us to submit to God, resist the devil, and draw near.
Do you see the movement?
The invitation to intimacy is surrounded by the call to surrender.
And that changes everything.
Because the biblical invitation is not simply, “Come closer so you can feel better.”
It is, “Come to the God whose grace is greater than your sin, and stop pretending your sin is harmless.”
There is a difference between wanting God to comfort your conscience and allowing God to transform your heart.
And that difference can be painful.
Especially when the thing God is confronting is the thing you have spent years justifying.
Maybe it's the bitterness you call discernment.
Maybe it's the pride you call confidence.
Maybe it's the relationship you keep defending even though you know it is pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe it's the secret habit that has slowly become your refuge whenever life hurts.
Maybe it's the dishonesty you excuse because you're afraid of what the truth might cost you.
Or maybe it's something quieter.
You have become so busy doing things associated with God that you barely spend time with God Himself.
You know how to post Scripture.
You know how to encourage others.
You know how to appear spiritually strong.
But behind the screen…
Behind the smile…
Behind the familiar “I'm blessed”…
You are tired of pretending.
And somewhere deep inside, you wonder whether the Lord would still welcome you if everything hidden were brought into the light.
Listen carefully.
The answer to that question is found not in your ability to manufacture a spotless past, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Yet to understand the invitation properly, we need to listen to what James actually wrote.
In the original Greek, the opening command of James 4:8 is:
ἐγγίσατε τῷ θεῷ, καὶ ἐγγιεῖ ὑμῖν
Engisate tō Theō, kai engiei hymin.
“Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.”
The verb ἐγγίσατε (engisate) is an imperative from the Greek verb engizō, meaning to approach or come near.
James is issuing a command.
He is calling his readers to respond.
And the following verb, ἐγγιεῖ (engiei), expresses the promise that God will draw near to them.
But the next two commands are just as important:
καθαρίσατε χεῖρας, ἁμαρτωλοί, καὶ ἁγνίσατε καρδίας, δίψυχοι.
Katharisate cheiras, hamartōloi, kai hagnisate kardias, dipsychoi.
“Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”
James is drawing on the biblical language of cleansing and purity.
The hands point naturally toward conduct—what we do.
The heart points toward our inward life—our desires, motives, and loyalties.
And the word δίψυχοι (dipsychoi) is especially revealing.
It literally combines the ideas of “two” and “soul” or “inner life.”
It describes someone divided in allegiance, unstable in devotion.
James also uses this word in James 1:8 when speaking of a double-minded person.
This does not mean that every Christian who experiences doubt, anxiety, temptation, or emotional struggle is automatically living in deliberate rebellion.
James is confronting divided loyalty.
The heart that tries to hold on to God while refusing to release what stands against Him.
And perhaps that is why this verse cuts so deeply.
Because we know what it feels like to be divided.
To love Jesus and still wrestle with temptation.
To desire holiness and still fall.
To long for peace while repeatedly returning to things that steal it.
To want God's will until His will challenges something we desperately want to keep.
But here is where we must be careful.
James is not teaching that sinners must make themselves morally perfect before God will receive them.
If that were the message, none of us could approach Him.
The very passage begins with the declaration that God gives more grace.
The call to cleanse our hands and purify our hearts is a call to genuine repentance, not a demand to purchase God's acceptance through flawless behavior.
Scripture is clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace does not leave us unchanged (Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:11–12).
We do not repent to make Jesus willing to save us.
We repent because the Savior calls sinners to turn to Him.
We do not earn cleansing through religious performance.
We come to the One whose blood cleanses us from sin.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Notice who is faithful to forgive.
God.
Notice who cleanses.
God.
And notice what we are called to do.
Confess.
Stop hiding.
Stop defending the darkness.
Bring it into the light.
That is why the next verse in James is so uncomfortable.
James 4:9 says:
“Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.” (KJV)
Those are not words designed to make a casual reader comfortable.
But neither are they a command for Christians to live in perpetual misery.
James is addressing people who have treated serious sin with spiritual carelessness.
He calls them to recognize the weight of what they have been doing.
There is a kind of laughter that comes from genuine joy in the Lord.
And there is a kind of laughter that comes from refusing to take evil seriously.
James is confronting the second.
He is not condemning happiness.
He is confronting unrepentance.
Because sometimes the first evidence that a heart is awakening is that it can no longer laugh at what once seemed harmless.
The joke stops being funny.
The excuse stops sounding convincing.
The secret stops feeling safe.
And suddenly the person who has spent years saying, “It's not that serious,” begins to whisper…
“Lord, what have I done?”
That moment can be terrifying.
But it can also become the beginning of restoration.
Second Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance leading to salvation, from worldly sorrow, which produces death.
Not every tear is repentance.
And repentance does not always arrive with tears.
The issue is not how dramatic our emotions become.
The issue is whether sorrow turns us toward God.
Worldly sorrow may grieve over consequences, embarrassment, or exposure.
Godly sorrow recognizes sin for what it is and turns toward the mercy of God.
One can leave a person trapped in shame.
The other leads toward the Savior.
And perhaps nowhere is that distinction more beautifully illustrated than in one of the most heartbreaking stories Jesus ever told.
A young man demanded his inheritance from his father.
Then he left home.
He wanted the father's gifts without the father's presence.
He wanted freedom without accountability.
He wanted the pleasures of a distant country without considering what would happen when the money ran out.
And for a while, everything probably seemed wonderful.
Until it didn't.
The inheritance disappeared.
A famine came.
The friends, the pleasures, the illusion of control…
None of them could save him.
Eventually he found himself feeding pigs, so hungry that he longed for their food.
And then Luke 15:17 records a remarkable turning point:
“And when he came to himself…” (KJV)
What a phrase.
He came to himself.
The illusion broke.
He finally saw the truth.
He had traded the security of his father's house for a freedom that left him starving.
And he decided to return.
Not with a speech about how unfair life had been.
Not with excuses.
But with a confession.
He had sinned against heaven and before his father.
Yet while he was still a great way off, his father saw him.
And ran.
And embraced him.
And kissed him.
The son had prepared to ask for the place of a servant.
But the father called for a robe, a ring, sandals, and a celebration.
Do not miss the beauty of this.
The son did not return because he had already repaired everything he had broken.
He returned because he finally stopped running.
And the father's welcome revealed a mercy greater than the son's shame.
That parable is not a promise that every earthly relationship will be restored immediately, or that repentance removes every consequence.
It is a revelation of God's joy over the sinner who repents.
Jesus Himself says there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).
And this is why James 4:8 must never be preached without the Gospel.
Because if all we hear is “Cleanse your hands,” we may begin to imagine that Christianity is simply a desperate attempt to scrub ourselves clean enough to deserve God's love.
But the cross tells a different story.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, came into a world of sinners.
He did not merely deliver moral advice from a safe distance.
He entered our brokenness.
He endured rejection.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was crucified.
And on that cross, He bore our sins, accomplishing what our religious effort could never accomplish.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” (KJV)
Read those final words again.
“That he might bring us to God.”
There is the heart of the invitation.
Jesus did not die merely so that we could feel spiritual during a worship song.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
The way back is not paved with our perfection.
It is opened through His sacrifice.
Hebrews 10:19–22 connects our confidence to enter God's presence with the blood of Jesus and calls believers to draw near with sincere hearts and the assurance of faith.
And the Greek verb used for drawing near in Hebrews 10:22, προσερχώμεθα (proserchōmetha), is not the same verb James uses.
Yet the passages beautifully complement each other.
James calls us away from divided loyalty and toward humble repentance.
Hebrews reminds us that our confidence in approaching God rests upon the priestly work of Christ.
Together they protect us from two dangerous distortions.
Grace without repentance becomes permission to remain unchanged.
Repentance without grace becomes an exhausting attempt to save ourselves.
But biblical Christianity offers something infinitely better.
A Savior who forgives sinners and transforms them.
A Lord who welcomes the repentant and teaches them to walk in holiness.
A Redeemer who does not excuse our sin, yet does not abandon those who come to Him in faith.
And that brings us to the words immediately after James 4:9.
Words so beautiful that they should never be separated from the hard ones before them.
James 4:10 says:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” (KJV)
There it is.
The destination of the passage.
Not humiliation without hope.
Not endless condemnation.
Not spiritual despair.
Humility before the Lord.
And His promise to lift up the humble.
The Greek says:
ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον κυρίου, καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς.
Tapeinōthēte enōpion Kyriou, kai hypsōsei hymas.
“Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.”
The word ταπεινώθητε (tapeinōthēte) calls for humbling oneself.
The promise ὑψώσει (hypsōsei) means that He will lift up or exalt.
This is not a guarantee of immediate financial success, public recognition, or the disappearance of earthly suffering.
James is not offering a formula for worldly advancement.
He is declaring that God honors humility rather than pride.
And what a breathtaking reversal that is.
The world tells you to protect your image.
Jesus calls you to walk in truth.
The world tells you never to admit weakness.
The Gospel teaches you to depend upon grace.
The world tells you that being exposed is the end of your story.
But in Christ, confession and repentance can become the beginning of a new chapter.
Maybe the most dangerous thing you have been doing is not the sin itself alone.
Maybe it is the exhausting effort to keep that sin hidden while maintaining the appearance that everything is fine.
Because secrecy can become a prison.
And pride can make the prison feel like protection.
You learn to smile at church.
You learn which Bible verses to post.
You learn how to say “God is good” while avoiding the conversation you know you need to have.
You become skilled at managing what people see.
But when the room grows quiet and the phone screen goes dark…
You know.
You know the thing you keep returning to.
You know the apology you keep postponing.
You know the forgiveness you keep resisting.
You know the truth you have been afraid to face.
And perhaps tonight, the Holy Spirit is using these ancient words to confront something you have kept buried.
Not so that you will despair.
But so that you will stop running from the One who can forgive and restore you.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not permission to make peace with sin.
It is freedom from the crushing verdict that sin deserves, because Christ has borne it for those who belong to Him.
And Romans 8 continues by describing life through the Spirit.
The Gospel does not merely change our standing before God.
It begins changing the way we live.
So what does drawing near to God actually look like when you have failed?
Sometimes it looks like closing the app that keeps feeding your temptation.
Sometimes it looks like finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it looks like ending a pattern of deception and accepting the consequences.
Sometimes it looks like asking forgiveness without adding a long explanation of why you were justified.
Sometimes it looks like seeking help from a mature Christian, pastor, or trusted counselor because you know the battle has become too heavy to fight in isolation.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of avoidance.
And sometimes it looks like kneeling beside your bed with no eloquent prayer left.
Only these words:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no magic in the length of the prayer.
No special power in the volume of your voice.
The power belongs to the Savior to whom you are praying.
The tax collector in Luke 18:13 could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
He pleaded:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (KJV)
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the self-righteous Pharisee who trusted in his own goodness.
Why?
Because the way to God is not self-exaltation.
It is humble dependence upon His mercy.
And if you are reading this while carrying years of regret, there is something else you need to hear.
Your past may have consequences.
Some relationships may need time to heal.
Some trust may need to be rebuilt.
Some wounds may require patient care, accountability, and difficult conversations.
Grace does not erase the need for responsibility.
But your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
The apostle Paul once persecuted the church.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
David committed grievous sins and faced painful consequences.
Their stories are not identical, and Scripture does not minimize what they did.
But each reveals, in different ways, that human failure is not greater than God's power to show mercy and accomplish His purposes.
And above every human testimony stands the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The One who makes redemption possible.
The One who turns enemies into reconciled children of God.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because the past never matters.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the sin that brought us down.
He is able to forgive.
He is able to restore.
He is able to transform.
And He is worthy of the life we once tried to live without Him.
Maybe that is why you needed to read beyond the first half of James 4:8.
You came looking for a promise that God would come near.
And you found a call to surrender.
But hidden inside that confrontation was a mercy you might have missed.
God does not invite you to keep pretending.
He invites you to come into the light.
Not because the light will flatter you.
But because the light reveals the truth.
And Jesus Christ is the Savior who meets repentant sinners with grace.
Not as a test of how spiritual you appear.
Not because a public comment can prove the condition of your soul.
But because sometimes an honest conversation begins when someone finally admits they are struggling.
What is harder for you right now: trusting that God will forgive you, or surrendering the thing you know He is calling you to release?
You don't have to expose private details.
You don't have to tell strangers what belongs in a confidential conversation with a trusted person.
Someone else may need to hear that repentance and restoration are possible.
Let this become more than another article people read and forget.
Let it become a place where struggling believers can encourage one another to return to Christ.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't ignore that thought.
Perhaps it is a brother who has quietly withdrawn from fellowship.
A sister who feels disqualified because of her past.
A friend who has stopped praying because shame convinced them that God no longer wants to hear their voice.
Or someone who has never understood why Christians speak so passionately about the grace of Jesus.
You never know who is silently searching for a reason to believe that coming home to God is still possible.
Not because the article itself has power.
But because the Word of God deserves to be revisited long after an emotional moment has passed.
Return to James 4:1–10.
Read the entire passage.
Examine your heart.
Pray over it.
And let Scripture, not merely an inspirational quotation, shape your understanding of repentance and grace.
This is also why we continue building Gospel Warrior.
Not simply to produce more Christian content.
But to keep placing Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who desperately need the truth of Jesus Christ.
Some are new believers trying to understand the Bible.
Some are parents searching for resources to strengthen their families.
Some are exhausted Christians trying to rebuild neglected spiritual habits.
Some are people who have been wounded, confused, or discouraged and are looking for trustworthy biblical encouragement.
And some are still standing at the edge of faith, wondering whether the Gospel could truly change a life like theirs.
We want those resources to remain accessible.
Because biblical nourishment should not become a privilege reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, strengthened your understanding of Scripture, or helped you return to the Lord in a difficult season, I want to invite you to consider something meaningful.
Not because a financial contribution proves your faith.
God's grace cannot be purchased, and no Christian should be made to feel that paying a ministry is a condition of glorifying Him.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a sincere act of generosity and partnership in the work of making biblical truth available to others.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully—not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is a voluntary ministry contribution, not a substitute for every biblical responsibility connected with tithes, offerings, or supporting your local church.
There are real costs involved in maintaining, developing, and expanding ministry resources.
It is the opportunity to stand alongside a ministry seeking to point people toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, spiritual growth, and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
If you are financially able, believe in this mission, and want to help it continue reaching more people, prayerfully consider becoming a monthly supporter here:
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Use the free resources.
A sincere prayer, a thoughtful comment, a personal invitation, or a Facebook share can help bring biblical encouragement to someone who might otherwise never encounter it.
And your generosity, whatever form it takes, should flow from love rather than fear.
Because the message we are carrying is not that people can buy their way closer to God.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to draw near through His grace.
That is the message worth protecting.
That is the Gospel worth sharing.
And that is why we keep pointing people back to the cross.
But before this ends, I want to return to the verse where we began.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Perhaps you have been reading those words for years while imagining that God was waiting for you to become impressive enough to approach Him.
Perhaps you thought you needed to fix every weakness, defeat every temptation, and silence every painful memory before you could pray with confidence.
But the Gospel says our hope rests in Christ.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come ready to turn from sin.
Come trusting in the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not confuse admiration for Christian teaching with saving faith.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
He is not merely an example to admire.
He is the Lord to whom we must surrender and the Savior in whom we must trust.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, do not let pride keep you in the distant country.
Return.
Confess.
Seek His forgiveness.
Take the next faithful step.
There is no promise that obedience will be painless.
But there is a Savior who is faithful.
A High Priest who understands our weakness.
A Lord whose mercy is greater than the darkness we are finally willing to confess.
Maybe tonight there will be no dramatic music.
No extraordinary sign.
No sudden emotional rush.
Maybe there will only be a quiet room, an open Bible, and a tired heart finally telling the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have been divided. I have defended things I should have surrendered. I have sought comfort while resisting Your correction. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I place my trust in You. Lead me in the truth. Amen.”
And tomorrow, keep walking.
Keep reading.
Keep praying.
Keep obeying.
Keep depending on grace.
Because drawing near to God is not a technique for producing a momentary feeling.
It is a life of faith and repentance, made possible through Jesus Christ.
James began by exposing the conflict within the human heart.
He confronted pride.
He called for surrender.
He commanded repentance.
And then he left us with a promise:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.”
So don't stop reading at the comforting half of the verse.
Read the confrontation.
Read the call to repentance.
Read the promise of grace.
And above all, look to the Savior who makes reconciliation with God possible.
Because sometimes the words that wound our pride are the very words God uses to awaken our hearts.
The door you were afraid to approach was opened by the Savior who gave His life to bring you home.
